sem_data.subject: BCA-5002 Java Programming
sem_data.topic: Unit II — Java Collections Framework: Hierarchy, List, Set, Map & Iterators
detailed_notes: The Java Collections Framework (JCF) provides a unified architecture for representing, manipulating, and storing groups of objects. Situated in the 'java.util' package, it reduces programming effort, increases performance, and establishes high-level interoperability between unrelated APIs.

Core Collection Hierarchy Structure:
The framework is organized into two distinct interface root hierarchies:
1. java.util.Collection: The root interface for collections of individual elements. It branches into:
   - List: An ordered, index-based collection that permits duplicate elements. Implementations: ArrayList (dynamic resizable array, fast random access O(1), slow insertion/deletion O(N)), LinkedList (doubly linked list, fast insertion/deletion O(1), slow sequential access O(N)), Vector (thread-safe, synchronized equivalent of ArrayList, slower due to lock contention), and Stack (LIFO subclass of Vector).
   - Set: An unordered collection that contains NO duplicate elements. Implementations: HashSet (backed by HashMap, O(1) average lookup, no order guarantee), LinkedHashSet (maintains insertion order via doubly linked list), and TreeSet (implements NavigableSet/SortedSet, backed by Red-Black tree, elements sorted naturally or via Comparator, O(log N) operations).
   - Queue / Deque: Collections designed for holding elements prior to processing. Implementations: PriorityQueue (min-heap ordering), ArrayDeque (resizable array double-ended queue, faster than Stack/LinkedList).
2. java.util.Map: A completely separate root interface (does NOT inherit from Collection) mapping unique keys to values. Implementations: HashMap (hash table, O(1) average, permits one null key), LinkedHashMap (maintains insertion order), TreeMap (Red-Black tree, keys sorted, O(log N)), and Hashtable (legacy, synchronized, null keys/values strictly prohibited).

Cursors / Iterators in Java:
• Iterator: Universal forward-only cursor for any Collection (hasNext(), next(), remove()).
• ListIterator: Bidirectional cursor exclusive to List implementations (hasPrevious(), previous(), add(), set()).

sem_data.memorize: Root interfaces: Collection (List, Set, Queue) and Map (Key-Value, separate tree). ArrayList = Resizable Array O(1) access; LinkedList = Doubly Linked List O(1) insert; HashSet = O(1) no order; TreeSet = O(log N) sorted; HashMap = O(1) hash table.
sem_data.understand: Why is Map not a Collection? A Collection is a collection of individual elements (values), whereas a Map is a collection of key-value pairs (entries). Treating keys and values as a single element breaks standard Collection operations like add(Object) and contains(Object).
sem_data.common_mistakes: 1. Stating that Map implements the Collection interface (Map is a separate root interface). 2. Modifying a Collection directly while iterating over it with a for-each loop (throws ConcurrentModificationException; use Iterator.remove() instead).

model_answer_paragraphs: The Java Collections Framework (JCF), introduced in JDK 1.2, provides a standardized, high-performance architecture for data structures. It decouples core interfaces from concrete implementations, allowing developers to write flexible algorithms that operate on abstract collections rather than specific implementations. The framework is divided into two primary root hierarchies: java.util.Collection and java.util.Map.

• List Interface: Preserves insertion order, accessible via zero-based integer index. Permits duplicates. Key classes: ArrayList (ideal for frequent reads via contiguous memory), LinkedList (ideal for frequent insertions at arbitrary positions via pointers), and Vector (legacy synchronized thread-safe array).
• Set Interface: Unordered collection prohibiting duplicate elements. HashSet uses hash codes for O(1) lookups; LinkedHashSet maintains insertion order via a linked list; TreeSet guarantees sorted ascending order via Red-Black trees.
• Map Interface: Maps unique keys to values. HashMap provides O(1) lookups using bucket hashing and treeification of collided buckets; TreeMap maintains sorted keys in O(log N) time.

While both ArrayList and Vector implement List using internal arrays, their concurrency and memory growth models diverge fundamentally. Vector's methods are declared 'synchronized', acquiring intrinsic object locks on every call, making it thread-safe but introducing severe performance penalties in single-threaded programs. ArrayList is unsynchronized and fast. Furthermore, when capacity is exhausted, Vector doubles its size (100% expansion), whereas ArrayList grows by 50% (newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)), consuming memory more conservatively.

• Iterator: Can traverse any Collection in the forward direction only using hasNext() and next(). It supports safe in-place element removal via remove().
• ListIterator: Exclusive to List implementations. It supports bidirectional traversal using previous() and hasPrevious(), allows element modification via set(obj), element insertion via add(obj), and index inspection via nextIndex() and previousIndex().

apt_data.topic: Time & Work — Foundations, One-Day Work Concept & The LCM Efficiency Method
tutorial: Time and Work problems are based on the principle of inverse proportionality: if a person can complete a total work in 'n' days, then in 1 day they complete exactly (1 / n)th part of the work.

The Two Classical Problem-Solving Methods:
1. The Traditional Unitary / Fractional Method: Work is taken as 1 whole unit. If A takes 10 days and B takes 15 days, 1-day combined work = (1/10) + (1/15) = (3 + 2)/30 = 5/30 = 1/6. Total days = 6 days.
2. The Professional LCM Efficiency Method (The Preferred Placement Strategy):
Instead of working with cumbersome fractions, assume Total Work = LCM of individual days.
Efficiency = (Total Units of Work) / (Days Taken).
Example: A takes 10 days, B takes 15 days. Total Work = LCM(10, 15) = 30 units.
• A's daily efficiency = 30 / 10 = 3 units/day.
• B's daily efficiency = 30 / 15 = 2 units/day.
Combined daily efficiency = 3 + 2 = 5 units/day.
Total time taken together = Total Work / Combined Efficiency = 30 / 5 = 6 days instantly!

Man-Days Equivalence Formula (Chain Rule):
(M1 * D1 * H1) / W1 = (M2 * D2 * H2) / W2, where M = workers, D = days, H = hours/day, W = work done.
apt_data.formulas:
1. LCM Efficiency: Total Work = LCM(days); Efficiency = Work / Time
2. Combined Work of Two Persons: Time = (A * B) / (A + B)
3. Combined Work of Three Persons: Time = (A * B * C) / (AB + BC + CA)
4. Chain Rule: (M1 * D1 * H1 * E1) / W1 = (M2 * D2 * H2 * E2) / W2
apt_data.shortcut:
The Product-over-Sum Shortcut for Two Workers:
If A takes 12 days and B takes 24 days:
Combined Time = (A * B) / (A + B) = (12 * 24) / (12 + 24) = 288 / 36 = 8 days instantly!
apt_data.recognition: Look for 'A can do a piece of work in X days and B in Y days', 'A and B working together can do a piece of work in...', or 'A is twice as efficient as B'.
apt_data.p1_q: [Foundation] A can complete a work in 12 days, and B can complete the same work in 24 days. In how many days can both of them together complete the work?
apt_data.p1_s:
Method 1: Product-over-Sum Shortcut:
Time = (A * B) / (A + B) = (12 * 24) / (12 + 24) = 288 / 36 = 8 days.
Method 2: LCM Efficiency Verification:
Total Work = LCM(12, 24) = 24 units.
- A's efficiency = 24 / 12 = 2 units/day.
- B's efficiency = 24 / 24 = 1 unit/day.
Combined efficiency = 2 + 1 = 3 units/day.
Days needed = 24 / 3 = 8 days.
Answer: 8 days.
apt_data.p2_q: [Standard Placement] A and B together can do a piece of work in 10 days. A alone can do it in 15 days. In how many days can B alone complete the work?
apt_data.p2_s:
Step 1: Total Work = LCM(10, 15) = 30 units.
Step 2: Calculate daily efficiencies:
- (A + B)'s combined efficiency = 30 / 10 = 3 units/day.
- A's individual efficiency = 30 / 15 = 2 units/day.
Step 3: B's individual efficiency = Combined - A = 3 - 2 = 1 unit/day.
Step 4: Time taken by B alone = Total Work / B's efficiency = 30 / 1 = 30 days.
Alternative Shortcut: Time_B = (Combined * A) / (A - Combined) = (10 * 15) / (15 - 10) = 150 / 5 = 30 days.
Answer: 30 days.
apt_data.p3_source: [VERIFIED PUBLIC COMPANY QUESTION — TCS NQT / Cognizant GenC Quantitative]
apt_data.p3_q: A can do a piece of work in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work together for 5 days, and then A leaves. In how many more days will B finish the remaining work?
apt_data.p3_s:
Step 1: Determine Total Work via LCM:
Total Work = LCM(20, 30) = 60 units.
Step 2: Calculate individual efficiencies:
- A's efficiency = 60 / 20 = 3 units/day.
- B's efficiency = 60 / 30 = 2 units/day.
Combined efficiency = 3 + 2 = 5 units/day.
Step 3: Work completed in first 5 days together:
Work done = 5 days * 5 units/day = 25 units.
Step 4: Calculate remaining work after A leaves:
Remaining Work = 60 - 25 = 35 units.
Step 5: Time taken by B alone to finish remaining work:
Time = Remaining Work / B's efficiency = 35 / 2 = 17.5 days (or 17 1/2 days).
Answer: 17.5 days.
apt_data.p4_q: [Hard / Time-Pressure] A is twice as good a workman as B, and together they finish a piece of work in 18 days. In how many days will A alone finish the work?
apt_data.p4_s:
Step 1: Ratio of efficiencies:
A is twice as good as B ==> Efficiency A : Efficiency B = 2 : 1.
Let B's efficiency = 1 unit/day, then A's efficiency = 2 units/day.
Step 2: Combined efficiency = 2 + 1 = 3 units/day.
Step 3: Calculate Total Work:
They finish the work together in 18 days:
Total Work = Combined Efficiency * Days = 3 units/day * 18 days = 54 units.
Step 4: Time taken by A alone:
Time_A = Total Work / A's efficiency = 54 / 2 = 27 days.
Time taken by B alone = 54 / 1 = 54 days.
Answer: 27 days.
timed_set: A can do a work in 15 days, B in 20 days, and C in 30 days. In how many days will all three finish it together?
12 men can complete a project in 16 days. In how many days can 8 men complete the same project?
A is thrice as efficient as B and is able to finish a job in 60 days less than B. Find time taken together.
A can finish a work in 18 days and B in 15 days. B worked for 10 days and left. In how many days can A finish remaining work?
If 3 men or 6 women can do a piece of work in 16 days, in how many days will 12 men and 8 women do it?
timed_solutions: LCM(15, 20, 30) = 60. Efficiencies: A=4, B=3, C=2. Total = 9. Days = 60 / 9 = 20 / 3 = 6.67 days. Answer: 6.67 days.
Efficiency 3:1 ==> Time 1:3. Difference = 2 units = 60 days ==> 1 unit = 30 days (A=30, B=90). Together = (30 * 90) / 120 = 2700 / 120 = 22.5 days. Answer: 22.5 days.
Work = 90. A=5, B=6. B does 10 * 6 = 60 units. Remaining = 30 units. A takes 30 / 5 = 6 days. Answer: 6 days.
3 Men = 6 Women ==> 1 Man = 2 Women. 12 Men + 8 Women = 24 + 8 = 32 Women. W1 * D1 = W2 * D2 ==> 6 * 16 = 32 * D2 ==> D2 = 96 / 32 = 3 days. Answer: 3 days.
apt_data.trap: Do not confuse efficiency ratio with time ratio! Efficiency is INVERSELY proportional to time: if Efficiency is 2 : 1, then Time is 1 : 2.
